metadata.title: Rewrite Rule Inference Using Equality Saturation

nodes.name: Magma
nodes.statement: A \emph{magma} is a set $G$ equipped with a binary operation $\diamond: G \times G \to G$. A \emph{homomorphism} $\varphi : G \to H$ between two magmas is a map such that $\varphi(x \diamond y) = \varphi(x) \diamond \varphi(y)$ for all $x,y \in G$. An \emph{isomorphism} is an invertible homomorphism.
nodes.label: magma-def

nodes.name: Free Magma
nodes.statement: The \emph{free magma} $M_X$ generated by a set $X$ (which we call an \emph{alphabet}) is the set of all finite formal expressions built from elements of $X$ and the operation $\diamond$. An element of $M_X$ will be called a \emph{word} with alphabet $X$. The \emph{order} of a word is the number of $\diamond$ symbols needed to generate the word. Thus for instance $X$ is precisely the set of words of order $0$ in $M_X$.
nodes.label: free-magma-def

nodes.statement: For a finite alphabet $X$, the number of words of order $n$ is $C_n |X|^{n+1}$, where $C_n$ is the $n^{\mathrm{th}}$ Catalan number and $X$ is the cardinality of $X$.
Follows from standard properties of Catalan numbers.

nodes.name: Induced homomorphism
nodes.statement: Given a function $f: X \to G$ from an alphabet $X$ to a magma $G$, the \emph{induced homomorphism} $\varphi_f: M_X \to G$ is the unique extension of $f$ to a magma homomorphism. Similarly, if $\pi \colon X \to Y$ is a function, we write $\pi_* \colon M_X \to M_Y$ for the unique extension of $\pi$ to a magma homomorphism.
nodes.label: induced-def

nodes.name: Law
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a set. A \emph{law} with alphabet $X$ is a formal expression of the form $w \simeq w'$, where $w, w' \in M_X$ are words with alphabet $X$ (thus one can identify laws with alphabet $X$ with elements of $M_X \times M_X$). A magma $G$ \emph{satisfies} the law $w \simeq w'$ if we have $\varphi_f( w ) = \varphi_f ( w' )$ for all $f: X \to G$, in which case we write $G \models w \simeq w'$.
nodes.label: law-def

nodes.name: Models
nodes.statement: A \emph{theory} is a set $\Gamma$ of laws. Given a theory $\Gamma$, a magma $G$ is a \emph{model} of $\Gamma$ with the (overloaded) notation $G\models\Gamma$ if $G\models w\simeq w'$ for every $w\simeq w'$ in $\Gamma$; we also say that $G$ \emph{satisfies} $\Gamma$. Given a law $E$, we write $\Gamma \models E$ if every magma $G$ that models $\Gamma$, also models $E$.
nodes.label: models-def

nodes.name: Derivation
nodes.statement: Given a theory $\Gamma$ and a law $w\simeq w'$ over a fixed alphabet $X$, we say that $\Gamma$ \emph{derives} $w\simeq w'$, and write $\Gamma\vdash w\simeq w'$, if the law can be obtained using a finite number of applications of the following rules: \begin{enumerate} \item if $w\simeq w' \in \Gamma$, then $\Gamma\vdash w\simeq w'$. \item $\Gamma\vdash w\simeq w$ for any word $w$. \item if $\Gamma\vdash w\simeq w'$, then $\Gamma\vdash w'\simeq w$. \item if $\Gamma\vdash w\simeq w'$ and $\Gamma\vdash w'\simeq w''$, then $\Gamma\vdash w\simeq w''$. \item if $\Gamma\vdash w\simeq w'$, then $\Gamma\vdash \varphi_f(w) \simeq \varphi_f(w')$ for every $f: X \to M_X$. \item if $\Gamma\vdash w_1\simeq w_2$ and $\Gamma\vdash w_3\simeq w_4$, then $\Gamma\vdash w_1 \diamond w_3\simeq w_2\diamond w_4$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: derivation-def

nodes.name: Birkhoff's completeness theorem
nodes.statement: For any theory $\Gamma$ and words $w, w'$ over a fixed alphabet $$ \Gamma\vdash w\simeq w'\ \mathrm{iff}\ \Gamma\models w\simeq w'.$$
nodes.label: sound-complete

nodes.statement: (Sketch) The `only if' component is soundness, and follows from verifying that the rules of inference in \Cref{derivation-def} holds for $\models$. The `if' part is completeness, and is proven by constructing the magma of words, quotiented out by the relation $\Gamma \vdash w \simeq w'$, which is easily seen to be an equivalence relation respecting the magma operation.

nodes.name: Compactness theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a theory, and let $E$ be a law. Then $\Gamma \models E$ if and only if there exists a finite subset $\Gamma'$ of $\Gamma$ such that $\Gamma' \models E$.
nodes.label: compactness-thm

nodes.statement: The claim is obvious for $\models$, and the claim then follows from \Cref{sound-complete}.

nodes.name: Pushforward
nodes.statement: Let $w \simeq w'$ be a law with some alphabet $X$, $G$ be a magma, and $\pi: X \to Y$ be a function. If $G \models w \simeq w'$, then $G \models \pi_*(w) \simeq \pi_*(w')$. In particular, if $\pi$ is a bijection, the statements $G \models w \simeq w'$ and $G \models \pi_*(w) \simeq \pi_*(w')$ are equivalent.
nodes.label: push

nodes.statement: Trivial.

nodes.name: Equivalence
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a magma and $X$ be an alphabet. Then the relation $G \models w \simeq w'$ is an equivalence relation on $M_X$.
nodes.label: equiv

nodes.statement: Trivial.

nodes.name: Counting laws up to relabeling
nodes.statement: Up to relabeling, the number of laws $w \simeq w'$ of total order $n$ is $C_{n+1} B_{n+2}$.
nodes.label: law-count

nodes.statement: Follows from the properties of Catalan and Bell numbers.

nodes.name: Counting laws up to relabeling and symmetry
nodes.statement: Up to relabeling and symmetry, the number of laws $w \simeq w'$ of total order $n$ is $$ C_{n+1} B_{n+2}/2$$ when $n$ is odd, and $$ (C_{n+1} B_{n+2} + C_{n/2} (2D_{n+2} - B_{n+2}))/2$$ when $n$ is even, where $D_n$ is the number of partitions of $[n]$ up to reflection.
nodes.label: law-count-sym

nodes.statement: Elementary counting.

nodes.name: Counting laws up to relabeling, symmetry, and triviality
nodes.statement: Up to relabeling, symmetry, and triviality, the number of laws of total order $n$ is $$ C_{n+1} B_{n+2}/2$$ if $n$ is odd, $2$ if $n = 0$, and $$ (C_{n+1} B_{n+2} + C_{n/2} (2D_{n+2} - B_{n+2}))/2 - C_{n/2} B_{n/2+1}$$ if $n \geq 2$ is even.
nodes.label: law-count-triv

nodes.statement: Routine counting.

nodes.name: Implication
nodes.statement: A law $E$ is said to \emph{imply} another law $E'$ if $\{E\} \models E'$, or equivalently: $$ G \models w \simeq w' \implies G \models w'' \simeq w''' \hbox{ for all magmas } G$$ Two laws are said to be \emph{equivalent} if they imply each other.
nodes.label: impl

nodes.name: Pre-order
nodes.statement: If we define $E \leq E'$ if $E$ implies $E'$, then this is a pre-order on the set of laws, and equivalence is an equivalence relation.
nodes.label: pre-order

nodes.statement: Trivial.

nodes.label: maximal

nodes.name: Minimal element

nodes.name: Duality of laws
nodes.statement: The law $w \simeq w'$ implies $w''\simeq w'''$, if and only if $w^{\mathrm{op}} \simeq (w')^{\mathrm{op}}$ implies $w''^{\mathrm{op}} \simeq (w''')^{\mathrm{op}}$.
nodes.label: duality

nodes.statement: This follows from the fact that a magma $G$ satisfies a law $w \simeq w'$ if and only if $G^{\mathrm{op}}$ satisfies $w^{\mathrm{op}} \simeq (w')^{\mathrm{op}}$.

nodes.name: Diagonalization
nodes.statement: An equational law of the form \begin{equation} F(x_1,\dots,x_n) = G(y_1,\dots,y_m), \end{equation} where $x_1,\dots,x_n$ and $y_1,\dots,y_m$ are distinct elements of the alphabet, implies the diagonalized law $$ F(x_1,\dots,x_n) = F(x'_1,\dots,x'_n).$$ where $x'_1,\dots,x'_n$ are distinct from $x_1,\dots,x_n$ In particular, if $G(y_1,\dots,y_m)$ can be viewed as a specialization of $F(x'_1,\dots,x'_n)$, then these two laws are equivalent.
nodes.label: diag

nodes.statement: From two applications of \Cref{prediag} one has $$ F(x_1,\dots,x_n) = G(y_1,\dots,y_m)$$ and $$ F(x'_1,\dots,x'_n) = G(y_1,\dots,y_m)$$ whence the claim.

nodes.name: Laws implied by the constant law
nodes.statement: If $w, w'$ each have order at least one, then the law $w \simeq w'$ is implied by the constant law (46). If exactly one of $w, w'$ has order zero, and the law $w \simeq w'$ is not implied by the constant law.
nodes.label: constant-impl

nodes.statement: Routine.

nodes.name: Criterion for implication
nodes.statement: If $w \simeq w'$ is such that every variable appears the same number of times in both $w$ and $w'$, and $w \simeq w'$ implies another law $w'' \simeq w'''$, then every variable appears the same number of times in both $w''$ and $w'''$.
nodes.label: variable-impl

nodes.statement: Consider the magma $\mathrm{MS}$ of multisets over an arbitrary set $A$ (which can be seen as finitely supported maps $A\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$), with the multiset addition law $+$. By hypothesis, this magma satisfies $w \simeq w'$, and hence $w'' \simeq w'''$, giving the claim by comparing the orders of the elements of $A$ appearing in $w''$ and $w'''$ in this magma.

nodes.name: 387 implies 43
nodes.statement: 387 implies 43.
nodes.label: 387_implies_43

nodes.statement: (From \href{https://mathoverflow.net/a/450905/766}{MathOverflow}). By \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?387}{E387}, one has the law \begin{equation} (x \diamond x) \diamond y = y \diamond x. \end{equation} Specializing to $y=x \diamond x$, we conclude $$(x \diamond x) \diamond (x \diamond x) = (x \diamond x) \diamond x$$ and hence by another application of \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?387}{E387} we see that $x \diamond x$ is idempotent: \begin{equation} (x \diamond x) \diamond (x \diamond x) = x \diamond x. \end{equation} Now, replacing $x$ by $x \diamond x$ in \Cref{387-again} and then using \Cref{idem} we see that $$ (x \diamond x) \diamond y = y \diamond (x \diamond x)$$ so in particular $x \diamond x$ commutes with $y \diamond y$: \begin{equation} (x \diamond x) \diamond (y \diamond y) = (y \diamond y) \diamond (x \diamond x). \end{equation} Also, from two applications of \Cref{387-again} one has $$(x \diamond x) \diamond (y \diamond y) = (y \diamond y) \diamond x = x \diamond y.$$ Thus \Cref{op-idem} simplifies to $x \diamond y = y \diamond x$, which is \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?43}{E43}.

nodes.name: 29 equivalent to 14
nodes.statement: 29 is equivalent to 14.
nodes.label: 29_equiv_14

nodes.statement: By \Cref{duality} it suffices to show that \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?29}{E29} implies \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?14}{E14}. From \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?29}{E29} one has $$ x = ((x \diamond y) \diamond x) \diamond (x \diamond y)$$ and also $$ y = (x \diamond y) \diamond x$$ giving $x = y \diamond (x \diamond y)$, which is \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?14}{E14}.

nodes.statement: By hypothesis, one has $$x \diamond y = (x \diamond z) \diamond (w \diamond y) $$ for all $x,y,z,w$. Various specializations of this give \begin{align} x \diamond y &= (x \diamond z) \diamond (y \diamond y) \\ x \diamond z &= (x \diamond z) \diamond (x \diamond z) \\ (x \diamond z) \diamond y &= ((x \diamond z) \diamond (x \diamond z)) \diamond (y \diamond y) . \end{align} \Cref{381-2} gives \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?3722}{E3722}, while \Cref{381-1}, \Cref{381-2}, \Cref{381-3} gives $$ x \diamond y = (x\diamond z) \diamond y$$ which is \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?381}{E381}.

nodes.name: 1689 is equivalent to 2
nodes.statement: 1689 is equivalent to \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?2}{E2}.
nodes.label: 1689_equiv_2

nodes.statement: The implication of \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?1689}{E1689} from \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?2}{E2} is trivial. The converse is a surprisingly long chain of implications; see pages 326--327 of \cite{Kisielewicz2}. With some computer assistance, we found the following human-readable proof. We denote $y^1=y$ and $y^{n+1}=y^n\diamond y$ for $n\geq 1$. We also introduce the notation \begin{equation} f(x,y) = (x \diamond y) \diamond y , \qquad g(x,y) = x\diamond f(x,y) = x \diamond ((x \diamond y) \diamond y) . \end{equation} The initial equation states $x = (y \diamond x) \diamond f(x,z)$. Our main step will be to prove that for all $t\in M$ there exists $w\in M$ such that $f(t,w) = t$. The rest of the proof is then straightforward. Indeed, the initial equation gives $t = (y \diamond t) \diamond f(t,w) = (y \diamond t) \diamond t = f(y,t)$ for any $t,y\in M$. With such a simple expression of $f$ the initial equation becomes $x = (y \diamond x) \diamond z$, which easily implies the singleton law, for instance by writing $x = ((y \diamond w) \diamond x) \diamond z = w \diamond z$ for any $w,x,y,z \in M$. There remains to prove $f(t,w) = t$ for a well-chosen $w \in M$, explicitly, $w=g(t,t^5)=t\diamond t^7$. For any $t,u,v \in M$, the combinations $x = f(t,u)$ and $y = v \diamond t$ satisfy $y \diamond x = t$. Inserting these values into the initial equation yields the identity \begin{equation} f(t,u) = t \diamond f(f(t,u),z) . \end{equation} Specialize to $z=f(u,v)$ and note that $f(t,u) \diamond z = (\cdots \diamond u) \diamond f(u,v) = u$ by the initial equation so that $f(f(t,u),z) = (f(t,u) \diamond z) \diamond z = u \diamond z = g(u,v)$. Inserting this into \eqref{Kisielewicz-tfftuz} yields \begin{equation} f(t,u) = t \diamond g(u,v) . \end{equation} On the one hand, \eqref{Kisielewicz-tfftuz} with $z=u=t$ states that $t^3 = t \diamond t^5$, so (using $f(t^n,t)=t^{n+2}$) \begin{equation} f(t,t^5) = (t \diamond t^5) \diamond t^5 = t^3 \diamond t^5 = t^3 \diamond f(t^3,t) = g(t^3,t) , \end{equation} and \eqref{Kisielewicz-ftg} with $(u,v)=(t^3,t)$ then implies $f(t,t^3) = t \diamond g(t^3,t) = t \diamond f(t,t^5) = g(t,t^5)$. On the other hand, \eqref{Kisielewicz-ftg} with $(u,v)=(t,t^5)$ implies $t^3 = t \diamond g(t,t^5)$. We deduce \begin{equation} f(t,g(t,t^5)) = (t \diamond g(t,t^5)) \diamond g(t,t^5) = t^3 \diamond f(t, t^3) = (\cdots \diamond t) \diamond f(t,\dots) = t . \end{equation}

nodes.name: Consequences of 1571
nodes.statement: Magmas satisfying 1571 also satisfy \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?2662}{E2662}, \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?40}{E40}, \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?23}{E23}, \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?8}{E8}, \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?16}{E16}, \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?14}{E14}, \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?43}{E43}, and \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?4512}{E4512}, and are in fact abelian groups of exponent two. Conversely, all abelian groups of exponent two satisfy \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?1571}{E1571}.
nodes.label: 1571_impl

nodes.statement: Suppose that a magma $G$ satisfies \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?1571}{E1571}, thus \begin{equation} x = (y \diamond z) \diamond (y \diamond (x \diamond z)). \end{equation} $$ x = ((x \diamond y) \diamond (x \diamond y)) \diamond ((x \diamond y) \diamond (x \diamond (x \diamond y)))$$ and $$ x = (x \diamond y) \diamond (x \diamond (x \diamond y))$$ whence $$x = ((x \diamond y) \diamond (x \diamond y)) \diamond x$$ which is \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?2662}{E2662}. This gives $$y = ((y \diamond z) \diamond (y \diamond z)) \diamond y$$ while from \Cref{1571-again} one has $$ (y \diamond z) \diamond (y \diamond z) = (x \diamond y) \diamond (x \diamond ((y \diamond z) \diamond (y \diamond z) \diamond y))$$ whence $$ (x \diamond y) \diamond (x \diamond y) = (y \diamond z) \diamond (y \diamond z).$$ This implies that $(x \diamond y) \diamond (x \diamond y)$ does not depend on $x$, or on $y$, hence is equal to some constant $e$: $$ (x \diamond y) \diamond (x \diamond y) = e.$$ From \Cref{1571-again} the magma operation is surjective, hence \begin{equation} x \diamond x = e \end{equation} which gives \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?40}{E40}. Applying \Cref{1571-again} with $x=y=z$ we conclude $$ x = e \diamond (x \diamond e)$$ while if we instead take $y=z=e$ we have $$ x = e \diamond (e \diamond (x \diamond e))$$ hence $$ x = e \diamond x$$ and then also $$ x = x \diamond e$$ from which we readily conclude \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?23}{E23}, \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?8}{E8}; thus $e$ is an identity element. From \Cref{1571-again} with $z=e$ we now have \begin{equation} x = y \diamond (y \diamond x) \end{equation} which is \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?16}{E16}. If instead we take $y=e$ we have \begin{equation} x = z \diamond (x \diamond z) \end{equation} which is \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?14}{E14}. So if we substitute $z = x \diamond y$ and use \Cref{16-again} we obtain $$ x = (x \diamond y) \diamond y$$ and hence $$ y \diamond x = y \diamond ((x \diamond y) \diamond y) = x \diamond y$$ thanks to \Cref{14-again}. This gives \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?43}{E43}, thus $G$ is now commutative. From \Cref{1571-again} once more one has $$x \diamond (y \diamond z) = (y \diamond x) \diamond (z \diamond ((x \diamond (y \diamond z)) \diamond x))$$ which one can simplify using commutativity and \Cref{16-again} (or \Cref{14-again}) to eventually obtain $$x \diamond (y \diamond z) = (x \diamond y) \diamond z$$ which is \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?4512}{E4512}. $G$ is now commutative and associative, and every element is its own inverse and of exponent $2$, hence is an abelian group thanks to \Cref{xxe}, so $G$ is an abelian group of exponent $2$ as claimed. The converse is easily verified.

nodes.name: 953 is equivalent to 2
nodes.statement: 953 is equivalent to \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?2}{E2}.
nodes.label: 953_equiv_2

nodes.statement: It suffices to show that \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?953}{E953} implies \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?2}{E2}. Pick an element $0$ of $G$ and define $1 = 0 \diamond 0$ and $2 = 1 \diamond 1$ (we do not require $0,1,2$ to be distinct). From \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?953}{E953} with $x=z=0$ we have $$ 0 = y \diamond 2.$$ If we then apply \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?953}{E953} with $z=1$ we conclude that $$ x = y \diamond 0$$ for all $x,y$, from which one concludes $x=x'$ for any $x,x' \in G$, giving \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?2}{E2}.

nodes.name: Sheffer stroke axiom
nodes.statement: Definition 345169 axiomatizes the Sheffer stroke operation $x \diamond y = \overline{xy}$ in a Boolean algebra.
nodes.label: sheffer

nodes.statement: See \cite{mccune_et_al}. In fact this is the shortest law with this property. A sketch of proof follows. One can easily verify that the Sheffer stroke operation satisfies this law. Conversely, if this law holds, then automated theorem provers can show that the three Sheffer axioms $$ (x \diamond x) \diamond (x \diamond x) = x$$ $$ x \diamond (y \diamond (y \diamond y)) = x \diamond x$$ $$ (x \diamond (y \diamond z)) \diamond (x \diamond (y \diamond z)) = ((y \diamond y) \diamond x) \diamond ((z \diamond z) \diamond x)$$ are satisfied. A classical result of Sheffer \cite{sheffer} then allows one to conclude.

nodes.name: Natural central groupoid axiom
nodes.statement: 26302 characterizes natural central groupoids.
nodes.label: natural-central-groupoid

nodes.statement: See \cite[Theorem 5]{knuth}. The proof is quite lengthy; a sketch is as follows. It is easy to see that natural central groupoids satisfy \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?26302}{E26302}. Conversely, if this law holds, then \begin{align*} (y \diamond z) \diamond (z \diamond w) &= (( x \diamond ((w \diamond (y \diamond z)) \diamond w)) \diamond ((y \diamond z) \diamond w)) \diamond (z \diamond w)\\ &= z \end{align*} so we have a central groupoid. Setting $y = (t \diamond t) \diamond t$, $z = t \diamond (t \diamond t)$, $w = t \diamond t$ in \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?26302}{E26302} we also obtain $$ (x \diamond t) \diamond t = (t \diamond t) \diamond t.$$ Using the notation $$ x^{(1)} := (x \diamond x) \diamond x, \quad x^{(2)} := x \diamond (x \diamond x)$$ we then have \begin{align*} x \diamond t &= ((x \diamond x) \diamond (x \diamond t)) \diamond ((x \diamond t) \diamond t) \\ &= x \diamond t^{(1)}. \end{align*} A lengthy computer-assisted argument then gave the dual identity $$ t^{(2)} \diamond x = t \diamond x$$ Together, these give $$ x^{(2)} \diamond y^{(1)} = x \diamond y.$$ Multiplying on the left by $x = x^{(1)}\diamond x^{(2)}$, one can conclude that $$ x^{(2)} = x \diamond (x \diamond y).$$ One then has \begin{align*} (x \diamond y)^{(1)} &= ((y \diamond x) \diamond (x \diamond y)) \diamond (x \diamond y) \\ &= x \diamond (x \diamond y) \\ &= x^{(2)} \end{align*} and a similar argument gives $$ (x \diamond y)^{(2)} = y^{(1)}.$$ Since $(x \diamond x)^{(1)} = x^{(2)}$ and $(x \diamond x)^{(2)} = x^{(1)}$, we conclude that $x^{(1)}$ and $x^{(2)}$ are idempotent. Since $x = x^{(1)} \diamond x^{(2)}$, we see that every $x$ is the product of two idempotents. One can show that this representation is unique, and gives a canonical identification with a natural central groupoid.

nodes.name: Kisielewicz's first Austin law
nodes.statement: 374794 is an Austin law.
nodes.label: kis-thm

nodes.statement:
First we show that every finite model of \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?374794}{E374794} is trivial. Write $y^2 := y \diamond y$ and $y^3 := y^2 \diamond y$. For any $y,z$, introduce the functions ${f_y: x \mapsto y^3 \diamond x}$ and ${g_{yz}: x \mapsto x \diamond (y^2 \diamond z)}$. \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?374794}{E374794} says that $g_{yz}(f_y(x))=x$, hence by finiteness $g_{yz}=f_y^{-1}$, showing that $g_{yz}$ does not depend on the value of $z$. Since $$ f_y(y^2 \diamond z) = g_{yz}(y^3),$$ it follows that $f_y(y^2 \diamond z)=f_y(y^3)$ which by injectivity of $f_y$ implies that $z\mapsto y^2 \diamond z$ is a constant function (with $y$ fixed). Substituting $y^2$ for $y$ shows that the same is true for $z\mapsto (y^2 \diamond y^2) \diamond z$, and since $$ f_y(z) = (y^2 \diamond y) \diamond z = (y^2 \diamond y^2) \diamond z$$ we conclude that $f_y$ is also a constant function. But this function is already known to be injective, thus there do not exist distinct elements in its domain, showing that the model must be trivial. To construct an infinite model, consider the magma of positive integers $\mathbb{Z}^+$ with the operation $x \diamond y$ defined by $$ x \diamond y =  egin{cases} 2^y, & x= y \ 3^y, & x= 1,\ y 
eq 1 \ z, & x=3^z,\ y 
eq x \ 1, & else \end{cases}. $$ Then $y \diamond y = 2^y$ and $(y \diamond y) \diamond y = 1$ for all $y$. If $x
eq 1$ we have that $$ ((y \diamond y) \diamond y) \diamond x = 3^x, $$ and since $(y \diamond y) \diamond z$ is a power of two for all $y, z$ it follows that $$ 3^x \diamond ((y \diamond y) \diamond z) = x. $$ The case $x=1$ requires a further argument: observe that $w = (y \diamond y) \diamond z$ evaluates to one unless $z = 2^y$, in which case it evaluates to $2^{2^y}$ (which is greater than or equal to four). In particular, $w$ never takes the value two. Thus $$ (((y \diamond y) \diamond y) \diamond 1) \diamond ((y \diamond y) \diamond z) = 2 \diamond w = 1, $$ concluding our proof that this magma is a model of \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?374794}{E374794}

nodes.name: Kisielewicz's second Austin law
nodes.statement: 28770 is an Austin law.
nodes.label: kis-thm2

nodes.statement:
Using the $y^2$ and $y^3$ notation as before, the law reads  egin{equation} x = (y^3 \diamond x) \diamond (y \diamond z). \end{equation} In particular, for any $y$, the map $T_y \colon x \mapsto y^3 \diamond x$ is injective, hence bijective in a finite model $G$. In particular we can find a function $f : G 	o G$ such that $T_y f(y) = y^3$ for all $y$ Applying \Cref{kis2-law} with $x = f(y)$, we conclude $$ T_y(y \diamond z) = y^3 \diamond (y \diamond z) = f(y) $$ and thus $y \diamond z$ is independent of $z$ by injectivity of $T_y$. Thus, the right-hand side of \Cref{kis2-law} does not depend on $x$, and so the model is trivial. This shows there are no non-trivial finite models. To establish an infinite model, use $\mathbb{N}$ with $x \diamond y$ defined by requiring $$ y \diamond y = 2^y; \quad 2^y \diamond y = 3^y$$ and $$ 3^y \diamond x = 3^y 5^x$$ for $x 
eq 3^y$, and $$ (3^y 5^x) \diamond z = x$$ for $z 
eq 3^y 5^x$. Finally set $$ 2^{3^y} \diamond z = 3^y$$ for $z 
eq 3^y, 2^{3^y}$. All other assignments of $\diamond$ may be made almost arbitrarily, such as setting them to $1$. It is then a routine matter to establish \Cref{kis2-law}.

nodes.name: Equation 5093 has no non-trivial finite models
nodes.statement: \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?5093}{E5093} has no non-trivial finite models.
nodes.label: 5093-nontrivial

nodes.statement: From \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?5093}{E5093} we see that the map $w \mapsto y \diamond w$ is onto, hence injective in a finite model. Using this injectivity four times in \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?5093}{E5093}, we see that $z \diamond y$ does not depend on $z$, hence the expression $x \diamond (z \diamond y)$ does not depend on $x$. By \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?5093}{E5093} again, this means that $x$ does not depend on $x$, which is absurd in a non-trivial model.

nodes.name: Austin's finite model theorem
nodes.statement: Any law with at most two variables has a non-trivial finite model.
nodes.label: austin-two

nodes.statement: If neither side of the law is a single variable then the zero law $x \diamond y = 0$ will work, so one can assume the law takes the form $x = f(x,y)$. Consider a finite field $F$ with the operation $x \diamond y := ax+by$ for some coefficients $a,b \in F$. Then the law becomes a pair of equations $P(a,b)=0$, $Q(a,b)=1$ in the coefficients for some polynomials $P,Q$ with integer coefficients, which one can verify to not divide each other (they have the same degree, and do not have the same set of non-zero monomials). From Bezout's theorem, this equation has a solution in some field, and hence by the Lefschetz principle it has a solution in a finite field.
Let $X$ be finite, and let $f, g: X \to X$ be such that $f = f \circ f \circ g$. Then $f = f \circ g \circ f$.
nodes.label: ffg

nodes.statement: Call a point $x \in X$ \emph{periodic} if $f^n(x) = x$ for some $n>0$. Because the forward orbit $x, f(x), f^2(x), \dots$ in a finite space $X$ must repeat, we see that for each $x$ there exists an $n$ such that $f^n(x)$ is periodic. Let $n_x$ be the first $n$ for which this occurs. If $n_x > 1$, then $g(x), f(g(x)), f(f(g(x))$ cannot be periodic (as this would imply $f(x)$ periodic), and then we can see that $n_{g(x)} = n_x + 1$. Hence the maximal value of $n_x$ is at most $1$, which implies that $f(x)$ is periodic for every $x$. Thus there is an $n > 1$ such that $f^n = f$. Since $f = f^2 \circ g$, we have $f^n = f^{n-2} \circ f \circ f = f^{n-2} \circ (f^2 \circ g) \circ f = f^n \circ g \circ f = f \circ g \circ f$, as desired.
Let $X$ be finite, and let $f, g: X \to X$ be such that $f = g \circ f \circ f$. Then $f = f \circ g \circ f$.
nodes.label: gff

nodes.statement: By hypothesis, $f^2(x)$ uniquely determines $f(x)$. This prevents $n_x = 2$ for any $x$ (because if $n>2$ is such that $f^{n+2}(x) = f^2(x)$, then $f^{n+1}(x) \neq f(x)$), and hence also prevents $n_x > 2$ for any $x$. So again we have $f(x)$ periodic for all $x$, so $f^n = f$ for some $n>1$. Then $f = f^n = f \circ (g \circ f^2) \circ f^{n-2} = f \circ g \circ f^n = f \circ g \circ f$ as required.

nodes.name: Eventual period
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be finite and $f: X \to X$. Then there exists $n \geq 1$ such that $f^{2n} = f^n$.
nodes.label: period

nodes.statement: By the pigeonhole principle, there exists $n \geq 1$, $m \geq 0$ such that $f^{m+n} = f^m$, which implies on iteration that $f^{m+mn} = f^m$ and hence $f^{2mn} = f^{mn}$, giving the claim.

nodes.name: 3994 implies 3588 for finite models
nodes.statement: All finite magmas which satisfy 3994 also satisfy 3588.
nodes.label: finite_imp_3994_3588_thm

nodes.statement: For a finite magma $M$, consider the set $S = \{x \diamond y | x, y \in M\}$. Now $f_z : x \mapsto z \diamond x$ and $g_z : x \mapsto x \diamond z$. They both map $S$ to $S$, and due to the hypothesis $g_z \diamond f_z$ is the identity on $S$, so because $S$ is finite $f_z$ and $g_z$ must be inverse bijections on it, and therefore they commute.

nodes.name: 3994 does not imply 3588 for infinite models
nodes.statement: There exists a magma which satisfies \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?3994}{E3994} and not \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?3588}{E3588}.
nodes.label: non_imp_3994_3588_thm

nodes.statement: Consider $\mathbb{N}$, with $x \diamond y$ defined as $x \oplus y$ (bitwise XOR) if $x$ and $y$ are even, $y+2$ if only $y$ is even, $x \dot - 2$ if only $x$ is even, and $0$ if both are odd. Note that the range of the operation is the set of even naturals. \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?3994}{E3994} is satisfied, because for even $z$ we get $z \oplus (x \diamond y) \oplus z = x \diamond y$ and for odd $z$ we get $(x \diamond y) + 2 \dot - 2 = x \diamond y$. Setting $x = y = z = 1$, \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?3588}{E3588} isn't satisfied.

On a finite magma $M$, equation 3342, $x \diamond y= y \diamond (x \diamond (x \diamond x))$, implies equation 3522, $x \diamond y = x \diamond ((y \diamond y) \diamond y)$, as well as equation 4118, $x \diamond y = ((x \diamond x) \diamond x) \diamond y$.

Write $Sx := x \diamond$, $fx := x \diamond Sx$ and $Cx = Sx \diamond x$, then we have $x \diamond y= y \diamond fx$, and our task is to show $x \diamond y = Cx \diamond y$ and $x \diamond y = x \diamond Cy$ for finite magmas, giving the four open implications. Note that $x \diamond y= y \diamond fx = fx \diamond fy$, hence $f$ is a homomorphism. By \Cref{period}, there is $n \geq 1$ with $f^n = f^{2n}$. From 3342 we have $Sx = S fx$ and $Cx = Sx \diamond x = f^n Sx \diamond f^n x = f^n Sx \diamond f^{2n} x = f^{2n-1} x \diamond f^n Sx = f^{n-1} x \diamond S x = f(f^{n-1} x) = f^n x$. Then $$ Cx \diamond y = f^n x \diamond y = f^{2n} x \diamond f^n y = f^n x \diamond f^n y = x \diamond y$$ and a similar argument gives $x \diamond Cy = x \diamond y$.

nodes.name: 1167 implies 1096
nodes.statement: For finite magmas, Equation 1167, $$ x = y \diamond ((z \diamond (y \diamond y)) \diamond x)$$ implies Equation 1096, $$ x = y \diamond ((x \diamond (z \diamond y)) \diamond x).$$

We write 1167 as $$ L_y L_{z \diamond Sy} = I,$$ hence $L_y$ is invertible and $L_{z \diamond Sy} L_y = I$. In particular $L_{z \diamond Sy} Sy = y$, hence squaring is injective, hence surjective. So 1167 can be rewritten as $L_{S^{-1} y} L_{z \diamond y} = I$, hence $L_{z \diamond y}$ is independent of $z$. In particular $$ L_{x \diamond (z \diamond y)} = L_{S^{-2} z \diamond (z \diamond y)} = L_{L_{S^{-2} z} L_{S^{-1} z \diamond S S^{-2} z} y} = L_y$$ by 1167, hence the right-hand side of 1096 is independent of $z$. Replacing $z$ with $y$, the claim now follows from 1167.

nodes.name: 1133 implies 1167
nodes.statement: For finite magmas, Equation 1133, $$ x = y \diamond ((y \diamond (z \diamond y)) \diamond x)$$ implies Equation 1167, $$ x = y \diamond ((z \diamond (y \diamond y)) \diamond x).$$

1133 asserts that $L_y L_{y \diamond (z \diamond y)} = I$, hence $L_y$ is invertible and $L_{y \diamond (z \diamond y)} = L_y^{-1}$ does not depend on $z$. Setting $z = y \diamond Sy$ we see from 1133 that $y \diamond (z \diamond y) = y$ and hence we have left-involution: $L_y = L_y^{-1}$. Replacing $y$ with $L_z y$ in 1133 we now get $L_{L_z y} L_{L_z y \diamond y} = I$, which since $L_{L_z y}$ is its own inverse gives \begin{equation} L_{L_z y \diamond y} = L_{L_z y}. \end{equation} In particular $$ R_y^3 z = L_{L_z y \diamond y} y = L_{L_z y} y = R_y^2 z$$ hence as $L_{R_y^2 z}$ is its own inverse $$ y =L_{R_y^2 z} L_{R_y^2 z} y = L_{R_y^2 z} R_y^3 z = L_{R_y^2 z} R_y^3 z = S( R_y^2 z).$$ Thus squaring is surjective, hence invertible. Next, by \eqref{intermediate} we have $L_{z \diamond Sy} = L_w$ where $w = R_{Sy}^2 z$. By \eqref{intermediate} and the fact that $L_w$ is its own inverse, we have $$ L_w^2 w = w = L_{z \diamond Sy} Sy =L_w Sy,$$ hence $Sw = L_w w = Sy$. As $S$ is injective, we have $L_w = L_y$, and then $L_y L_{z \diamond Sy} = L_y^2 = I$, giving 1167.

nodes.name: 1441 implies 4067, 1443 implies 3055
nodes.statement: For finite magmas, Equation 1441, $$ x = (x \diamond y) \diamond (x \diamond (x \diamond x))$$ implies Equation 4067, $$ x \diamond x = ((x \diamond x) \diamond y) \diamond x,$$ and equation 1443, $$ x = (x \diamond y) \diamond (x \diamond (x \diamond z))$$ implies Equation 3055, $$ x = (((x \diamond x) \diamond y) \diamond x) \diamond x.$$

Write $\tilde C x = x \diamond Sx$, then 1441 asserts that $R_{\tilde Cx} R_y x = x$. Setting $$y=Sx$$ we get $x = S\tilde Cx$, so by finiteness $\tilde C Sx = x$. Replacing $x$ with $Sx$ in 1441 we conclude $R_x R_y Sx = Sx$ which is 4067. Clearly 1443 implies 1441, hence 4067 by the previous implication, so that 3055 simplifies to $x = Sx \diamond x$. Meanwhile, 1443 also implies $x = S(x \diamond (x \diamond z))$. On taking square roots and using $S \tilde C = x$, we obtain $x \diamond (x \diamond z) = \tilde Cx$. Applying this with $z = Sx$ we conclude $L_x \tilde Cx = \tilde Cx$, hence on replacing $x$ with $Sx$ we get $L_{Sx} x = x$ as required.

nodes.name: 1681 implies 3877, 1701 implies 1035
nodes.statement: For finite magmas, Equation 1681, $$ x = (y \diamond x) \diamond ((x \diamond x) \diamond x)$$ implies Equation 3877, $$ x \diamond x = (y \diamond (x \diamond x)) \diamond x,$$ and Equation 1701, $$ x = (y \diamond x) \diamond ((z \diamond x) \diamond x)$$ implies Equation 1035, $$ x = x \diamond ((y \diamond (x \diamond x)) \diamond x).$$

This is very similar to the previous proof. Write $Cx = Sx \diamond x$, then 1681 asserts $R_{Cx} L_y x = x$. Again setting $y=Sx$ yields $x=SCx$ hence $x = CSx$, and on replacing $x$ with $Sx$ in 1681 one obtains 3877. nodes.name: Asterix does not imply Obelix
nodes.statement: There exists a magma satisfying the Asterix law (\href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?65}{E65}) with carrier $\mathbb{Z}$ such that the left-multiplication maps $L_y: x \mapsto y \diamond x$ are not injective for any $y \in \mathbb{Z}$. In particular, it does not satisfy the Obelix law (1491).
nodes.label: asterix-obelix

nodes.statement: Note that $L_y (y+h) = y + h + f(h)$, so the injectivity of the left-multiplication maps is equivalent to the injectivity of the map $h \mapsto h + f(h)$. The non-injectivity then follows from \Cref{no-inject}. Note that the Obelix law clearly expresses $x$ as a function of $y$ and $L_y x = y \diamond x$, forcing injectivity of left-multiplication, so the Obelix law fails.

nodes.name: Asterix implies Obelix for finite magmas
nodes.statement: Any finite magma satisfying the Asterix law (\href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?65}{E65}) also is left-cancellative and satisfies the Obelix law (\href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?1491}{E1491}).

nodes.statement: From \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?65}{E65} we see the map $z \mapsto y \diamond z$ is surjective, hence injective on a finite magma; thus the magma is left-cancellative. Replacing $x$ by $y \diamond x$ in this law, we see that $$ y \diamond x = y \diamond ((y\diamond x) \diamond (y \diamond (y \diamond x)));$$ using injectivity, we conclude $$ x = (y\diamond x) \diamond (y \diamond (y \diamond x))$$ which is \href{https://teorth.github.io/equational_theories/implications/?1491}{E1491}.

This is well-defined by property (4). \item The function $x - f(x)$, which is defined on the same domain as $f$, is injective. \item If $x$ is in the domain of $f$ but $f(x)$ isn't in the domain, then $x - f(x)$ isn't in the domain or image of $f$. \end{itemize}

eq c$, then similarly $z \diamond' x$ is undefined, and $y \diamond' x$ is not equal to $c = z$, so we are ok in this case also. Law 3 is clearly unaffected, and it is also straightforward to check that Law 4 is also not invalidated (here it is essential that $d_i 
eq a$). Now we verify Law 1.  egin{itemize} \item Case 1: $x=c$. Then for $x \diamond' y$ to be defined we must have $y=e_i$ for some $i$, but then $x \diamond' (x \diamond' y) = c \diamond' d_i$ is undefined as $d_i

Then $d_i \diamond' (d_i \diamond' c)$ is either undefined or is equal to $e_i$, in which case Law 1 holds as $c \diamond' e_i = d_i$. \item Case 3: $x \diamond' y = c$. Then $x=a$ and $y=b$. Since $d_i 
eq a$ for all $i$, $x \diamond (x \diamond y)$ is undefined. \item Case 4: $x \diamond' (x \diamond' y) = c$. Then this case is covered by the previous seed. \end{itemize}

nodes.statement: Suppose that $\diamond$ is a partial solution, and $a \diamond b$ is currently undefined. Then there exists an extension $\diamond'$ of $\diamond$ for which $a \diamond' b$ is defined.

nodes.statement:
Set $a \diamond' b = c$ for some new element $c$. If $d_1,d_2,...,d_n$ are the elements for which $a \diamond d_i = b$, set $c \diamond' d_i = c'_i$ for some new element $c'_i$, and also set $d_i \diamond' c'_i = a$. If $d_i \diamond a$ is equal to some $e_i$, set $e_i \diamond' c'_i = c''_i$ and $c'_i \diamond' c''_i = d_i$, where $c''_i$ is equal to $a$ if $e_i = d_i$, or is some new element otherwise. One can verify that no collisions are caused by this construction (this is why we have to take $c''_i=a$ when $e_i=d_i$), and that Law 2 is preserved. We need to verify that these constructions preserve Law 1. There are several cases:  egin{itemize} \item $y=c$. Not possible since there are no right multiplications by $c$ defined. \item $x=c$. Not possible since it forces $y = d_i$, $x \diamond y = c'_i$ for some $i$. \item $y=c'_i$, $x = d_i$. True by construction. \item $y=c'_i$, $x 
eq d_i$. This forces $x = e_i 
eq d_i$ and $x \diamond' y = c''_i$, but then $x \diamond' (x \diamond' y)$ is undefined. \item $x=c'_i$. Not possible because this forces $x \diamond' y = d_i$, and $x \diamond' (x \diamond' y)$ will be undefined. (Here we use the fact that $e_i=d_i$ can only occur when $d_i 
eq a$, by Law 2.) \item $x = c''_i$ is new. Not possible as no left multiplications by $c''_i$ are defined. \item $y=c''_i$ is new. This forces $x = c'_i$ and $x \diamond' y = d_i$, but then $x \diamond' (x \diamond' y)$ is undefined. \item $x$ and $y$ are not new and $x \diamond y$ was undefined. nodes.name: Promoting to $E_1$
nodes.statement: If $(E_1,E_2,f)$ is a partial solution and $h \in E_2 \backslash E_1$, then there exists an extension $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$ of $(E_1,E_2,f)$ such that $h \in E'_1$.
nodes.label: add-E1

nodes.statement: This will be a greedy construction, but we have to introduce a rather large number of additional elements to ensure that certain non-degeneracy conditions are maintained (in particular, the new elements $h'$ introduced have to be such that $f^2(h') - h'$ avoids $E_2$ and hence $\mathbb{Z}^3$, which requires a certain amount of complexity in the construction). Let $\tilde E_2$ denote the set $E_2$ together with all the elements of the form $-h'$, $h' - f^2(h')$, and $f^2(h') - h'$ for $h' \in E_2 \backslash E_1$; this is $\mathbb{Z}^3$ with a finite number of additional elements. Let $a$ be an element of $\mathbb{Z}^3$ such that the quantities $$ \pm Ta, \pm(Ta + a)$$ are distinct from each other and from $$0, \pm h, \pm (h - f(h)), \pm (f^2(h)-h);$$ this is possible since $T, T+1$ are invertible. Next, we pick an $x \in \mathbb{Z}^3 \times \mathbb{Z}$ such that the quantities $$ \pm x, \pm x + Ta, \pm x - Ta, \pm 2 x + Ta, \pm x + Ta + a, \pm (h + x), \pm (h - f(h) + x), \pm (f^2(h)-h + x + Ta)$$ are all distinct from each other and from $\tilde E_2$; indeed, from the choice of $a$ (and the non-zero nature of $h$, $f(h)$, $h-f(h)$, and $f^2(h)-h$) there are only finitely many $x$ for which a collision can occur between any pair of these expressions. We now promote $\pm h, \pm x, \pm x + Ta, \pm x - Ta$ to $E_1$, and also promote $h+x$, $h - f^2(h)$, $\pm 2x + Ta$, $\pm x + Ta + a$ to $E_2$. That is to say, we define $$ E'_1 := E_1 \cup \{\pm h, \pm x, \pm x + Ta, \pm x - Ta\}$$ and $$ E'_2 := E_2 \cup \{ -h, \pm x, \pm x + Ta, \pm x - Ta, h + x, h - f^2(h), \pm 2x + Ta \}.$$ We then define an extension $f'$ of $f$ to $E'_2$ by setting \begin{align*} f'(\pm x) &:= a \\ f'(\pm x + Ta) &:= \pm x \\ f'(\pm x - Ta) &:= \mp x + Ta \\ f'(\pm x + Ta + a) &:= \pm x - Ta \\ f'(\pm 2x + Ta) &:= \pm x + Ta \\ f'(\pm x + Ta + a) &:= \pm x - Ta \\ f'(-h) &:= x + Ta \\ f'(h+x) &:= h \\ f'(h - f^2(h)) &:= -h. \end{align*} It is easy to see that $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$ satisfies properties (a), (b), (d). By construction, we have $$ f'( (f')^2(h') - h') = -h'$$ for $$ h' = \pm h, \pm x, \pm x+Ta, \pm x-Ta$$ giving property (c). By construction, the quantities $$ -h', h' - f^2(h'), f^2(h') - h'$$ are distinct from each other and lie outside of $\tilde E_2 \cup E'_2$ for $$ h' = h+x, h - f^2(h), \pm 2x + Ta, \pm x + Ta + a$$ while these quantities are distinct from each other and lie in $\tilde E_2 \backslash E'_2$ for $h' \in E_2 \backslash E'_1$ (note that this forces $h' \neq \pm h$). This gives property (e).

nodes.name: Promoting to $E_2$
nodes.statement: If $(E_1,E_2,f)$ is a partial solution and $h \in (\mathbb{Z}^3 \times \mathbb{Z}) \backslash E_2$, then there exists an extension $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$ of $(E_1,E_2,f)$ such that $h \in E'_2$.
nodes.label: add-E2

nodes.statement: Let $\tilde E_2$ denote the set $E_2$ together with all elements of the form \begin{equation} -h', h' - f^2(h'), f^2(h') - h' \end{equation} for some $h' \in E_2 \backslash E_1$; this is $\mathbb{Z}^3$ with a finite number of elements attached, and is symmetric around the origin. First suppose that $h$ lies outside of $\tilde E_2$. Then we can find $a \in \mathbb{Z}^3$ such that the quantities $$ -h, \pm (h - Ta)$$ are distinct from each other, and lie outside of $\tilde E_2$. We now promote $h$ to $E_2$, thus setting $$ E'_1 := E_1$$ and $$ E'_2 := E_2 \cup \{h\}$$ and define an extension $f'$ of $f$ to $E'_2$ by setting $$ f'(h) := a.$$ It is then a routine matter to check that $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$ is an extension of $(E_1,E_2,f)$. Now suppose that $h$ lies in $\tilde E_2$. Then $h$ is of one of the forms \Cref{hp-form} for some $h' \in E_2 \backslash E_1$. Suppose it is of the form $-h'$ or $f^2(h') - h'$. We invoke \Cref{add-E1} to promote $h'$ to $E_1$ by using a suitable extension $(E'_1,E'_2,f')$; and now $h$ will lie in $E'_2$, giving the claim. If instead $h$ is of the form $h'-f^2(h')$, then this procedure might not place $h$ in $E'_2$; but if it does not, it will be of the form $-h''$ for $h'' = f^2(h')-h' \in E'_2 \backslash E'_1$. Applying \Cref{add-E1} one more time to now promote $h''$ to $E_1$, we will obtain a larger extension $(E''_1,E''_2,f'')$ with $h \in E''_2$, giving the claim.
